questions.q: A calligrapher disliked reading criticism of his own community. With what example was he answered?
options: A customer who refuses to pay for poor work
Not quite. The article says: A teacher who points out faults in his lettering is helping him improve, not making him feel inferior.
A rival who copies his designs
Not quite. The article says: A teacher who points out faults in his lettering is helping him improve, not making him feel inferior.
A judge who awards a prize
Not quite. The article says: A teacher who points out faults in his lettering is helping him improve, not making him feel inferior.
A teacher who points out faults in his lettering is helping him improve, not making him feel inferior
Yes. Criticism builds a sense of reform.
questions.rationale: “If your teacher tells you about your shortcomings, will you say that my teacher is making me insecure and is creating a sense of inferiority in me?”

questions.q: Ali pointed out a mistake in a ruling by Caliph Umar. How did Umar respond?
options: He asked Ali to keep such views private
Not quite. The article says: He accepted it at once: “If it were not for Ali, Umar would have perished”.
He let the ruling stand to save face
Not quite. The article says: He accepted it at once: “If it were not for Ali, Umar would have perished”.
He accepted it at once: “If it were not for Ali, Umar would have perished”
Right. The adviser is better than the flatterer.
He referred the matter to others
Not quite. The article says: He accepted it at once: “If it were not for Ali, Umar would have perished”.
questions.rationale: “Although Umar was the Caliph and ruler, he immediately accepted it and said: If it were not for Ali, Umar would have perished.”

questions.article: Guiding One to a Purposeful Life
questions.q: Everyone sets his watch by the city clock tower, yet few look to God’s guidance in the same way. What reason does the article give?
options: The clock tower is older
Not quite. The article says: People are serious about knowing the time, which serves their worldly aims, but not about the life to come.
People do not trust what is free
Not quite. The article says: People are serious about knowing the time, which serves their worldly aims, but not about the life to come.
People are serious about knowing the time, which serves their worldly aims, but not about the life to come
Well read. Interest decides attention.
The guidance is harder to see than a clock
Not quite. The article says: People are serious about knowing the time, which serves their worldly aims, but not about the life to come.
questions.rationale: “People are serious in wanting to know the time, but not the Word of God… they have no ambitions for the future life.”

questions.q: After the war Japan learned industrial methods from others and later taught them to its own teachers. What lesson does the article draw?
options: One must be willing to learn humbly from others before rising – “we have to lose in order to gain”
Yes. Pride would have barred the way.
Only large nations can progress
Not quite. The article says: One must be willing to learn humbly from others before rising – “we have to lose in order to gain”.
Borrowed knowledge never lasts
Not quite. The article says: One must be willing to learn humbly from others before rising – “we have to lose in order to gain”.
Teachers should guard their secrets
Not quite. The article says: One must be willing to learn humbly from others before rising – “we have to lose in order to gain”.
questions.rationale: “If it had chosen not to recognize the supremacy of others at that crucial point in its development, and had felt too proud to go to them for help, it could never have had such resounding successes.”

questions.q: A minister advised the Caliph al-Mansur against a costly plan; the Caliph put the advice down to the minister’s background, went ahead, and had to stop. What does the article learn from this?
options: Weigh advice as advice; do not assume it springs from ill-will
Correct. The adviser may well be right.
A ruler’s first idea is best
Not quite. The article says: Weigh advice as advice; do not assume it springs from ill-will.
Costly plans should always be completed
Not quite. The article says: Weigh advice as advice; do not assume it springs from ill-will.
Never take advice from ministers
Not quite. The article says: Weigh advice as advice; do not assume it springs from ill-will.
questions.rationale: “We must look at someone’s advice as advice, we should not necessarily consider it as arising out of ill-will.”

questions.q: What does the article say real sacrifice consists of?
options: Making one’s efforts widely known
Not quite. The article says: Doing small, unnoticed constructive work over a long time, without fame or reward – like a seed or a foundation brick.
Working only where success is quick
Not quite. The article says: Doing small, unnoticed constructive work over a long time, without fame or reward – like a seed or a foundation brick.
Giving away everything in one day
Not quite. The article says: Doing small, unnoticed constructive work over a long time, without fame or reward – like a seed or a foundation brick.
Doing small, unnoticed constructive work over a long time, without fame or reward – like a seed or a foundation brick
Right. Not a single dramatic gesture.
questions.rationale: “Real sacrifice means taking a part so small and so inconspicuous in constructive work that it is almost invisible, and this, no matter how prolonged the period.”

questions.q: How does the article define “national character”?
options: Loyalty to a political party
Not quite. The article says: The capacity and will to put the nation’s interest above one’s own when the two clash.
Pride in one’s language and dress
Not quite. The article says: The capacity and will to put the nation’s interest above one’s own when the two clash.
The capacity and will to put the nation’s interest above one’s own when the two clash
Yes. Without it no nation advances.
Knowledge of national history
Not quite. The article says: The capacity and will to put the nation’s interest above one’s own when the two clash.
questions.rationale: “It is, to put it simply, the capacity and the will to hold the interests of the nation supreme in every sphere.”

questions.q: The first editor of a great national work of biography wore himself out and did not see it finished. What does the article take from his example?
options: Editors should be better paid
Not quite. The article says: Great undertakings need selfless, patient labour from people ready to remain obscure and not see the fruit.
Large projects should be avoided
Not quite. The article says: Great undertakings need selfless, patient labour from people ready to remain obscure and not see the fruit.
Great undertakings need selfless, patient labour from people ready to remain obscure and not see the fruit
Well reasoned. Others complete what one begins.
Such works are never worth the cost
Not quite. The article says: Great undertakings need selfless, patient labour from people ready to remain obscure and not see the fruit.
questions.rationale: “One must be willing to remain obscure. One must keep on working tirelessly knowing quite well that he will not be able to see the fruit of his hard work.”

questions.q: The book under review advises: “Live like the honeybee.” What does this mean?
options: Live only among your own kind
Not quite. The article says: Take what is good from every situation and ignore the thorns, wasting no time on complaint.
Work without ever resting
Not quite. The article says: Take what is good from every situation and ignore the thorns, wasting no time on complaint.
Store up more than you need
Not quite. The article says: Take what is good from every situation and ignore the thorns, wasting no time on complaint.
Take what is good from every situation and ignore the thorns, wasting no time on complaint
Exactly. Extract the nectar and move on.
questions.rationale: “‘Live like the honeybee’. That is, extract what is good for you and leave what is unwanted. Do not waste your time in complaints and protests.”

questions.q: Which qualities do the verses (3:133-134) ascribe to the God-fearing for whom Paradise is prepared?
options: They avoid all contact with people
Not quite. The article says: They give in good times and bad, restrain their anger, and forgive others.
They never make a mistake
Not quite. The article says: They give in good times and bad, restrain their anger, and forgive others.
They are wealthy, learned and well known
Not quite. The article says: They give in good times and bad, restrain their anger, and forgive others.
They give in good times and bad, restrain their anger, and forgive others
Well read. “God loves those who do good works.”
questions.rationale: “For those who spend, both in prosperity and adversity, who restrain their anger and are forgiving towards their fellow men—God loves those who do good works.”
